title: Samlaut Peasant Uprising Signals Growing Rural Discontent
reason: The Samlaut Uprising is a well-documented historical event: a peasant rebellion broke out on 2 April 1967 near Samlaut, Battambang Province, Cambodia, triggered by the government's forced/low-price rice-collection system ('ramassage du paddy') enforced by troops — angry peasants attacked and killed soldiers collecting rice. The Royal Cambodian government (under Sihanouk/Lon Nol) responded with violent military suppression (army sweeps, air force strafing/bombing of villages), with a death toll reported in the hundreds and thousands of villagers fleeing into the forest. It is widely regarded by historians (notably Ben Kiernan, who devoted a two-volume scholarly monograph, 'The Samlaut Rebellion and Its Aftermath, 1967-70: The Origins of Cambodia's Liberation Movement,' Monash Univ., 1975, to this exact event) as a foundational mobilization of rural discontent that fed directly into the Khmer Rouge's formal launch of armed struggle later in 1967-68. Independent (non-Wikipedia) corroboration was found on khmerization.blogspot.com, which confirms the Samlaut location, the land/rice-related grievances against provincial officials, and the rebellion's role in escalating into the civil war that the Khmer Rouge exploited. Multiple other independent leads (Kiernan's monograph listings on Google Books/HathiTrust/Semantic Scholar/Amazon/Goodreads, a ResearchGate peer-reviewed paper on Khmer Rouge state formation in NW Cambodia) all corroborate the same year, location, cause, and historical significance, though those specific pages did not load full text via WebFetch. All material details in the event description (location, trigger, suppression, death toll, and downstream link to Khmer Rouge mobilization) match.

title: Mass Refugee Crisis Develops Along Thai-Cambodian Border
reason: Independent sources (Wikipedia: Sa Kaeo Refugee Camp, Khao-I-Dang, Cambodian humanitarian crisis) confirm that following Vietnam's Dec 1978 invasion of Cambodia, hundreds of thousands of Cambodians fled toward the Thai border. By late 1979 roughly 750,000 had reached the frontier zone, and the crisis fully developed/peaked through 1980: Khao-I-Dang holding center reached its peak population of ~160,000 in March 1980; Sa Kaeo camp operated until July 1980; the massive 'land bridge' relief operation (UNHCR/ICRC/NGOs) ran Dec 1979-Sept 1980 distributing ~150,000 metric tons of food. Border camps (Sa Kaeo, Khao-I-Dang, Nong Chan, etc.) simultaneously served as bases/shelter for Khmer Rouge remnants and non-communist resistance groups (e.g., KPNLF, formed Oct 1979), consistent with the description. The refugee/camp situation persisted for over a decade (camps did not fully close until the early-to-mid 1990s, e.g. Khao-I-Dang closed 1993), matching the 'lasted over a decade' claim. While the crisis technically originated in 1979, 1980 is accurately described as when the crisis 'developed' into its full-scale, internationally-managed form (peak camp populations, major relief operations, resistance basing) -- so year, country, and material facts all hold.

France24 (Nov 2022), VOD English, CamboJA News, and a Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime report (Sept 2022) confirm Sihanoukville and Koh Kong special economic zones as hubs, tied to Chinese organized crime groups, with a government crackdown announced Aug 2022 (2,000+ rescued, 95 detained) and September 2022 raids freeing 1,000+ foreigners from Sihanoukville compounds. International media exposure of this industry in 2022 substantially damaged Cambodia's global reputation, matching the event description closely. Country, year, actors, locations, methods (crypto scams, romance fraud), and scale (thousands/tens of thousands trafficked) all check out.

title: Cambodia Begins Market Economy Transition with IMF Support
reason: Independently confirmed: the IMF approved its first Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility (ESAF) arrangement for Cambodia on May 6, 1994 (SDR 84 million over three years), explicitly supporting the Royal Cambodian Government's transition from a centrally-planned/socialist economy to a market economy — including privatization of state enterprises, trade liberalization (removal of import licensing/quantitative restrictions building on the 1989 foreign investment law), and financial sector reform. This IMF-backed liberalization coincided with the takeoff of Cambodia's garment export sector (essentially zero in 1994, growing to $1.1B in exports and 80,000+ workers by 1998/99) driven by new FDI incentives, matching the description's claim about attracting foreign investment particularly in garments. Independent economic literature also confirms rising income inequality (Gini rising from ~33.5% in 1990 toward ~37-40% through the 1990s/2000s) even as aggregate GDP growth accelerated, matching the description's final claim about growth-inequality divergence. All material elements (country, year, actor, mechanism, sectoral effect, distributional outcome) are corroborated.

verifications.reason: Confirmed from multiple independent sources: the IMF approved a first arrangement for Cambodia (structural adjustment support, ~84 million SDR) on 6 May 1994 under what became the Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility (ESAF), explicitly to support Cambodia's transition from a centrally planned to a market economy after the 1991 Paris Peace Agreements and 1993 elections. The Royal Government's medium-term program (backed by the March 1994 ICORC donor plan following Washington Consensus prescriptions) included macroeconomic stabilization, financial-sector reform, and structural reforms; a privatization law was adopted in December 1994, and trade liberalization proceeded alongside it. This matches the description's core claims (year, country, IMF-supported transition, privatization, trade liberalization, financial-sector development). The broader claims about foreign investment flowing into the garment sector and rising inequality alongside growth are also independently corroborated as consequences of this same transition process that took hold through the mid-to-late 1990s (garment sector FDI boom from the mid/late 1990s; inequality rising substantially "since the mid-1990s" per Wikipedia's Economy of Cambodia page), consistent with the description framing these as downstream effects of the transition begun in 1994 rather than events confined strictly to calendar year 1994. No off-limits domains were used.
